profile.name: Banamba
profile.tagline: The Saramaccan beauty dance of Suriname, featuring hip swings and rhythmic shaking.
profile.insight: At the 2016 Banamba Riddim Party in Paranam, dancers performed a genre born during the slavery era from Saramaccan African heritage.
profile.profile: Banamba, also known as bandámmba, is a traditional genre of dance and music from Suriname, historically termed the Saramaccan beauty dance. Originating during the slavery era from the African heritage of the Saramaccans, the dance involves solo or group performances centered on swinging hips and shaking buttocks. Today, it marks official occasions, welcomes guests, and features in competitions and battles across cities like Paramaribo.
profile.profile_long: Banamba, also called bandámmba, is a genre of dance and music from Suriname, historically referred to as the Saramaccan beauty dance or Saramaccaanse schoonheidsdans in Dutch. The genre originated during the slavery era, drawing directly from the African heritage preserved by the Saramaccans. Structurally, the dance can be executed either as a solo performance or within a group setting. Its primary and most recognizable movements involve the vigorous swinging of the hips and the shaking of the buttocks, performed to the characteristic banamba rhythm, known in Saramaccan as the banamba ridem. At the beginning of the 21st century, Banamba maintains a vibrant presence in daily and civic life. It is performed both as a form of entertainment and to mark important official occasions, such as welcoming guests to a village or celebrating when a child receives a traditional pangi cloth. Furthermore, the dance is highly popular for community challenges, battles, and festivals. Notable modern manifestations of this tradition include specific large-scale celebrations such as the 2016 Banamba Riddim Party held in Paranam, the 2022 Banamba Neti held in Pokigron, and recurring competitive events situated in Paramaribo. Institutional documentation also highlights its performance history, such as multiple presentations recorded by Winston Adaba Choreography on October 10, 2021. Despite its prominence in Surinamese cultural expression, detailed technical breakdowns of footwork, instrumentation, and posture remain unrecorded in formal sources.
